ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In the first quadrant, there is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the paper and pointing outward. In the second quadrant, there is a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right. In this plane, a particle with mass $m$ and charge $+q$ enters the uniform electric field from point P on the x-axis with an initial velocity $v_0$ perpendicular to the x-axis. The particle exits the electric field at point Q, making a $45^\circ$ angle with the y-axis. After some time, the particle exits perpendicular to the x-axis. The distance between O and P is given as $d$. (Neglect the gravitational force on the particle.)

1. Find the coordinates of point Q on the y-axis.
2. Find the magnitude of the magnetic induction of a uniform magnetic field.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the first quadrant, there is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the paper and pointing outward. In the second quadrant, there is a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right. In this plane, a particle with mass $m$ and charge $+q$ enters the uniform electric field from point P on the x-axis with an initial velocity $v_0$ perpendicular to the x-axis. The particle exits the electric field at point Q, making a $45^\circ$ angle with the y-axis. After some time, the particle exits perpendicular to the x-axis. The distance between O and P is given as $d$. (Neglect the gravitational force on the particle.) 1. Find the coordinates of point Q on the y-axis. 2. Find the magnitude of the magnetic induction of a uniform magnetic field.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the coordinate origin O is at the intersection of the two coordinate axes, the x-axis is horizontal to the right, and the y-axis is vertical upward. Point P is located on the x-axis to the left of O, the distance from P to O is d, and the initial velocity v0 of the particle at point P is vertically upward. In the second quadrant, electric-field arrows pointing horizontally to the right are drawn; in the first quadrant, dotted symbols are drawn, indicating that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface outward. Then reason: Take P=(-d,0) according to the coordinates. The particle is subjected to a constant force horizontally to the right in the electric field in the second quadrant; let the acceleration be a=qE/m. Thus the motion in the electric field is x=-d+(1/2)at^2, y=v0 t. When it reaches Q, Q is on the y-axis, so x=0, giving d=(1/2)at^2. Also, when the particle leaves the electric field, its velocity makes a 45° angle with the y-axis, and the direction is upward to the right, so vx=vy. There is no acceleration in the vertical direction, vy=v0; in the horizontal direction vx=at, so at=v0, namely t=v0/a. Substituting into d=(1/2)at^2 gives d=v0^2/(2a), so a=v0^2/(2d), t=2d/v0. Therefore the ordinate of Q is y=v0t=2d, hence Q=(0,2d). When entering the magnetic field in the first quadrant, the speed magnitude is v=sqrt(v0^2+v0^2)=sqrt(2)v0, and the direction is the 45° direction along +x and +y. A positive charge in a magnetic field perpendicular to the paper surface outward is subjected to a Lorentz force, with the initial force direction downward to the right; the center of the circular motion is downward to the right of Q, and the line from Q to the center makes a 45° angle with the coordinate axes, with length R. The ordinate of the center is 2d-R/sqrt(2). The particle later shoots out from the x-axis and its velocity is perpendicular to the x-axis, so at the exit point the velocity is vertical, the radius is horizontal, and the center and this exit point are at the same height as the x-axis, namely the ordinate of the center is 0. Thus 2d-R/sqrt(2)=0, obtaining R=2sqrt(2)d. From the radius formula in a magnetic field R=mv/(qB)=m sqrt(2)v0/(qB), solving gives B=mv0/(2qd).
